text: {"questions":[{"prompt":"A streaming algorithm processes an input stream of n distinct elements using a Count-Min sketch with width w and depth d, guaranteeing that for any element x, the estimated frequency f̂(x) satisfies f(x) ≤ f̂(x) ≤ f(x) + εn with probability at least 1-δ. The algorithm is modified to also output all elements with estimated frequency above threshold T using a heap of size k. If the adversary can choose duplicate-heavy distributions, what is the tightest bound on the worst-case output size of this modified algorithm, and how does it relate to the space lower bound for exact frequent items?","explanation":"The Count-Min sketch guarantees additive error εn, so elements with true frequency below T-εn may be reported if collisions inflate their estimate. In worst case, all n distinct elements could have true frequency 1 but appear to exceed T due to hash collisions, yielding output size Θ(n). The space lower bound for exact frequent items is Ω(n) for deterministic algorithms, but this streaming algorithm uses sublinear space O((1/ε)log(1/δ)) while potentially outputting linearly many false positives. The tradeoff shows probabilistic data structures sacrifice output size guarantees for space efficiency.","expectedAnswer":"Θ(n) in worst case; sublinear sketch space enables only probabilistic control over output size, creating a fundamental tradeoff with exact frequent items lower bounds","choices":["Θ(n) in worst case; sublinear sketch space enables only probabilistic control over output size, creating a fundamental tradeoff with exact frequent items lower bounds","Θ(k) bounded by heap size; the heap filters all sketch estimation errors before output","Θ(1/ε) determined by sketch width; output size matches the number of counter arrays","Θ(T/ε); threshold and error parameter jointly bound distinct elements exceeding T-εn"],"topic":"Worst-case time, output size and duplicate data","skillID":"Worst-case time, output size and duplicate data","objectiveID":"","objective":"Analyze algorithmic guarantees precisely","difficulty":5,"format":"Multiple Choice"},{"prompt":"Consider a comparison-based algorithm that must output all duplicates in an array of n elements where the number of distinct values is unknown but bounded by m. The algorithm uses a balanced BST with lazy deletion, inserting each element and checking for existing matches. After processing, it traverses to collect duplicates. If an adversary constructs inputs maximizing both time and output size, what is the tightest asymptotic bound on the product of worst-case time and output size, and under what condition does this product exceed the information-theoretic lower bound for sorting?","explanation":"Worst-case time is Θ(n log m) for BST operations. Output size is Θ(n) when all elements duplicate one value (adversary maximizes duplicates). The product is Θ(n² log m). Sorting requires Ω(n log n) comparisons; the product exceeds this when n log m > log n, i.e., when m = n^ω(1) or when duplicate structure creates output-dependent work. The key insight: output size and time interact multiplicatively, and for m polynomial in n, the product Θ(n² log n) dominates the sorting lower bound, showing duplicate reporting can be harder than sorting due to output size coupling.","expectedAnswer":"Θ(n² log m); exceeds sorting lower bound when m = n^ω(1) or when output-time coupling creates superlinear work per duplicate","choices":["Θ(n² log m); exceeds sorting lower bound when m = n^ω(1) or when output-time coupling creates superlinear work per duplicate","Θ(n log n); product is bounded by sorting complexity regardless of duplicates","Θ(nm); linear in distinct values with BST height dominating the interaction","Θ(n²); output size and time are independent, giving quadratic bound always below sorting lower bound"],"topic":"Worst-case time, output size and duplicate data","skillID":"Worst-case time, output size and duplicate data","objectiveID":"","objective":"Analyze algorithmic guarantees precisely","difficulty":5,"format":"Multiple Choice"}]}

text: {"questions":[{"prompt":"A streaming algorithm processes an input stream of n integers, each in [1, n²], and must report all duplicates using O(1) words of working memory (excluding output). The algorithm may make a single pass over the stream and may output results only at the end. What is the tightest achievable worst-case bound on the number of output integers (counting duplicates with multiplicity) that any correct algorithm must produce in the worst case?","explanation":"With O(1) words of memory, the algorithm cannot store Θ(n) distinct values to detect duplicates via hashing or sorting. By the pigeonhole principle, any set of n integers from [1, n²] could have anywhere from 0 to n-1 duplicates. However, the adversary can force output size: consider that the algorithm must be correct for all inputs. An adversary can present n distinct values first; the algorithm, having no memory to record them, cannot distinguish this from a stream where some values repeat later. But the key constraint is that the algorithm must output all duplicates. The critical analysis: with O(1) memory, the algorithm can only remember a constant number of values. The adversary can arrange that for any constant k, n-k values appear exactly once and k values appear twice, but the algorithm cannot track which. Actually, tighter: the information-theoretic argument shows that to guarantee finding all duplicates, the worst-case output size must be Ω(n) because the adversary can force Θ(n) duplicates that the algorithm cannot filter. Specifically, partition [1, n²] into n groups of size n. The adversary picks one element from each group to repeat. With O(1) memory, the algorithm cannot track which groups have been seen, so it must output all potential duplicates, yielding n outputs. This is tight: a simple algorithm outputs every element as a \"potential duplicate,\" achieving exactly n outputs.","expectedAnswer":"Θ(n)","choices":["Θ(1)","Θ(√n)","Θ(n)","Θ(n log n)"],"topic":"Worst-case time, output size and duplicate data","skillID":"1","objectiveID":"1","objective":"Analyze algorithmic guarantees precisely","difficulty":5,"format":"Multiple Choice"},{"prompt":"A deterministic comparison-based algorithm receives two sorted arrays A and B, each containing n elements with possible duplicates, and must output the sorted multiset intersection (elements appearing in both, with multiplicity equal to the minimum count in each). The algorithm may use O(1) additional space beyond the output. What is the optimal worst-case time complexity, and what complication arises from duplicate handling that affects this bound?","explanation":"The standard two-pointer merge-like intersection runs in O(n) time for distinct elements. With duplicates, we must advance pointers carefully: when A[i] = B[j], we output the element and must advance both pointers past all copies of that value in both arrays to avoid redundant outputs. This requires counting duplicates in each array at that value, which can be done by linear scans or by binary search since arrays are sorted. However, with O(1) space, we cannot use hash tables. The key tradeoff: using only comparisons and O(1) space, we can use exponential search or galloping to skip duplicate runs. In the worst case where all elements equal the same value, we must verify the minimum count is n, requiring Ω(n) time just to confirm. The optimal bound remains Θ(n): the two-pointer approach with careful advancement—when values match, advance both pointers by 1 and output once, continuing while values match—actually works correctly for multisets. Wait: for multiset intersection with multiplicity, when A[i]=B[j]=v, we output v once and need to know how many more v's exist in each to determine if additional outputs needed. With O(1) space and sorted order, we can scan: count v's in A starting at i, count v's in B starting at j, output v min(countA, countB) times, then advance both pointers past v's. This is Θ(n) total. The complication is that without random access or extra space, duplicate runs force sequential processing, but the linear bound holds. Actually, the subtlety: if we use only comparisons and no index arithmetic beyond incrementing, we cannot binary search. The worst-case remains Θ(n) because each element is examined constant times.","expectedAnswer":"Θ(n); duplicates force sequential processing of runs but do not asymptotically increase the bound","choices":["Θ(n); duplicates are handled by standard two-pointer without asymptotic penalty","Θ(n log n); duplicates require binary search to count multiplicities efficiently","Θ(n); duplicates force sequential processing of runs but do not asymptotically increase the bound","Θ(n²); each duplicate may require re-scanning the other array to verify multiplicities"],"topic":"Worst-case time, output size and duplicate data","skillID":"1","objectiveID":"1","objective":"Analyze algorithmic guarantees precisely","difficulty":5,"format":"Multiple Choice"}]}

questions.prompt: A streaming algorithm processes an input stream of n distinct elements using a Count-Min sketch with width w and depth d, guaranteeing that for any element x, the estimated frequency f̂(x) satisfies f(x) ≤ f̂(x) ≤ f(x) + εn with probability at least 1-δ. The algorithm is modified to also output all elements with estimated frequency above threshold T using a heap of size k. If the adversary can choose duplicate-heavy distributions, what is the tightest bound on the worst-case output size of this modified algorithm, and how does it relate to the space lower bound for exact frequent items?
questions.explanation: The Count-Min sketch guarantees additive error εn, so elements with true frequency below T-εn may be reported if collisions inflate their estimate. In worst case, all n distinct elements could have true frequency 1 but appear to exceed T due to hash collisions, yielding output size Θ(n). The space lower bound for exact frequent items is Ω(n) for deterministic algorithms, but this streaming algorithm uses sublinear space O((1/ε)log(1/δ)) while potentially outputting linearly many false positives. The tradeoff shows probabilistic data structures sacrifice output size guarantees for space efficiency.
questions.expectedAnswer: Θ(n) in worst case; sublinear sketch space enables only probabilistic control over output size, creating a fundamental tradeoff with exact frequent items lower bounds
choices: Θ(n) in worst case; sublinear sketch space enables only probabilistic control over output size, creating a fundamental tradeoff with exact frequent items lower bounds
Θ(k) bounded by heap size; the heap filters all sketch estimation errors before output
Θ(1/ε) determined by sketch width; output size matches the number of counter arrays
Θ(T/ε); threshold and error parameter jointly bound distinct elements exceeding T-εn

questions.prompt: Consider a comparison-based algorithm that must output all duplicates in an array of n elements where the number of distinct values is unknown but bounded by m. The algorithm uses a balanced BST with lazy deletion, inserting each element and checking for existing matches. After processing, it traverses to collect duplicates. If an adversary constructs inputs maximizing both time and output size, what is the tightest asymptotic bound on the product of worst-case time and output size, and under what condition does this product exceed the information-theoretic lower bound for sorting?
questions.explanation: Worst-case time is Θ(n log m) for BST operations. Output size is Θ(n) when all elements duplicate one value (adversary maximizes duplicates). The product is Θ(n² log m). Sorting requires Ω(n log n) comparisons; the product exceeds this when n log m > log n, i.e., when m = n^ω(1) or when duplicate structure creates output-dependent work. The key insight: output size and time interact multiplicatively, and for m polynomial in n, the product Θ(n² log n) dominates the sorting lower bound, showing duplicate reporting can be harder than sorting due to output size coupling.
questions.expectedAnswer: Θ(n² log m); exceeds sorting lower bound when m = n^ω(1) or when output-time coupling creates superlinear work per duplicate
choices: Θ(n² log m); exceeds sorting lower bound when m = n^ω(1) or when output-time coupling creates superlinear work per duplicate
Θ(n log n); product is bounded by sorting complexity regardless of duplicates
Θ(nm); linear in distinct values with BST height dominating the interaction
Θ(n²); output size and time are independent, giving quadratic bound always below sorting lower bound

questions.prompt: A streaming algorithm processes an input stream of n integers, each in [1, n²], and must report all duplicates using O(1) words of working memory (excluding output). The algorithm may make a single pass over the stream and may output results only at the end. What is the tightest achievable worst-case bound on the number of output integers (counting duplicates with multiplicity) that any correct algorithm must produce in the worst case?
questions.explanation: With O(1) words of memory, the algorithm cannot store Θ(n) distinct values to detect duplicates via hashing or sorting. By the pigeonhole principle, any set of n integers from [1, n²] could have anywhere from 0 to n-1 duplicates. However, the adversary can force output size: consider that the algorithm must be correct for all inputs. An adversary can present n distinct values first; the algorithm, having no memory to record them, cannot distinguish this from a stream where some values repeat later. But the key constraint is that the algorithm must output all duplicates. The critical analysis: with O(1) memory, the algorithm can only remember a constant number of values. The adversary can arrange that for any constant k, n-k values appear exactly once and k values appear twice, but the algorithm cannot track which. Actually, tighter: the information-theoretic argument shows that to guarantee finding all duplicates, the worst-case output size must be Ω(n) because the adversary can force Θ(n) duplicates that the algorithm cannot filter. Specifically, partition [1, n²] into n groups of size n. The adversary picks one element from each group to repeat. With O(1) memory, the algorithm cannot track which groups have been seen, so it must output all potential duplicates, yielding n outputs. This is tight: a simple algorithm outputs every element as a "potential duplicate," achieving exactly n outputs.
choices: Θ(√n)
Θ(n)
Θ(n log n)

questions.prompt: A deterministic comparison-based algorithm receives two sorted arrays A and B, each containing n elements with possible duplicates, and must output the sorted multiset intersection (elements appearing in both, with multiplicity equal to the minimum count in each). The algorithm may use O(1) additional space beyond the output. What is the optimal worst-case time complexity, and what complication arises from duplicate handling that affects this bound?
questions.explanation: The standard two-pointer merge-like intersection runs in O(n) time for distinct elements. With duplicates, we must advance pointers carefully: when A[i] = B[j], we output the element and must advance both pointers past all copies of that value in both arrays to avoid redundant outputs. This requires counting duplicates in each array at that value, which can be done by linear scans or by binary search since arrays are sorted. However, with O(1) space, we cannot use hash tables. The key tradeoff: using only comparisons and O(1) space, we can use exponential search or galloping to skip duplicate runs. In the worst case where all elements equal the same value, we must verify the minimum count is n, requiring Ω(n) time just to confirm. The optimal bound remains Θ(n): the two-pointer approach with careful advancement—when values match, advance both pointers by 1 and output once, continuing while values match—actually works correctly for multisets. Wait: for multiset intersection with multiplicity, when A[i]=B[j]=v, we output v once and need to know how many more v's exist in each to determine if additional outputs needed. With O(1) space and sorted order, we can scan: count v's in A starting at i, count v's in B starting at j, output v min(countA, countB) times, then advance both pointers past v's. This is Θ(n) total. The complication is that without random access or extra space, duplicate runs force sequential processing, but the linear bound holds. Actually, the subtlety: if we use only comparisons and no index arithmetic beyond incrementing, we cannot binary search. The worst-case remains Θ(n) because each element is examined constant times.
questions.expectedAnswer: Θ(n); duplicates force sequential processing of runs but do not asymptotically increase the bound
choices: Θ(n); duplicates are handled by standard two-pointer without asymptotic penalty
Θ(n log n); duplicates require binary search to count multiplicities efficiently
Θ(n); duplicates force sequential processing of runs but do not asymptotically increase the bound
Θ(n²); each duplicate may require re-scanning the other array to verify multiplicities

questions.prompt: Consider a comparison-based algorithm that must output all duplicates in an array of n elements where the number of distinct values is k = n^(2/3). The algorithm has access to a sorted order oracle that returns the rank of any element in the sorted order of distinct values in O(1) time, but cannot directly compare elements. What is the tightest worst-case time complexity for outputting the exact duplicate set, assuming the output size (number of duplicate pairs) is Θ(n)?
questions.explanation: This combines several constraints: comparison-based lower bounds don't directly apply due to the oracle, but we must still identify duplicates. With k = n^(2/3) distinct values and Θ(n) duplicate pairs, the distribution has Θ(n^(2/3)) buckets with average size Θ(n^(1/3)). The oracle gives us bucket IDs in O(1), so we can hash to buckets. However, we need exact duplicates, not just bucket collisions. Within each bucket, we must identify actual duplicates. The worst case: one bucket has Θ(n) elements (all same value), requiring Θ(n) output, but we need to detect this without explicit comparisons. Using the oracle, we can verify equality by checking if two elements have the same rank. The challenge is the adversarial distribution: Θ(n^(2/3)) buckets each with Θ(n^(1/3)) elements, all distinct within buckets. We must check all pairs within buckets to find duplicates, but there are none — yet we cannot know without checking. With the oracle, we can sort within buckets using the rank (stable sort by original index to break ties), taking O(n^(1/3) log n^(1/3)) per bucket, total O(n^(2/3) · n^(1/3) · (1/3)log n) = O(n log n). But we can do better: use the oracle to fingerprint and detect duplicates via hashing with verification. The tight bound is Θ(n): we must touch each element, and with careful hashing we achieve linear time. The oracle eliminates the Ω(n log n) comparison sort lower bound since we're not comparison-based for ordering, but duplicate detection still requires handling the adversarial case where all within-bucket comparisons are needed.
choices: Θ(n log log n)
Θ(n)
Θ(n log n)
